text.p: Base metals had a mixed session on the London Metal Exchange on Friday with copper and zinc higher but nickel, aluminium, lead and tin all ending lower.
Crude oil prices ended lower for the fifth straight day on Friday as bearish sentiment tightened its hold on a market shaken by steep losses this week.
The selling pushed the Commodity Research Bureau's index of 17 futures down another 0.53 point at 237.30, a 12-month low.

NYMEX crude ended lower for the fifth straight session Friday as bearish sentiment tightened its hold on the oil market which was still shaken by steep losses Thursday. December crude ended off 32 cents at $23.03 a barrel. Crude's losses weighed on refined products. December heating oil settled off 0.25 cent at 66.60 cents a gallon while Dec gasoline ended up a mere 0.09 cent at 64.70 cents a gallon.
"People are still a bit shell-shocked and nobody seems to want to buy crude with this new bearish market," said Al Lindseth, a trader with GSC Energy in Atlanta.
Crude's losses weighed on December heating oil, which ended down 0.25 cent at 66.60 cents a gallon. But December gasoline ended up 0.09 cent at 64.70 cents a gallon on low stockpiles.

CBOT wheat futures closed mixed with nearby December higher on fund buying, traders said. March ended higher but a new low was set early in that contract at $3.65-1/2 per bushel, down from the previous low of $3.67 set Thursday.
Traders said the stiff competition worldwide for wheat export business and renewed concern about the karnal bunt fungus continued to limit market rallies.
There was news Thursday that karnal bunt had been found in some Tennessee wheat which triggered concerns the fungus might surface in other soft red winter wheat areas.
"Karnal bunt didn't help wheat any," said Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter Reynolds.
Base metals snapped back from their lows by Friday's London Metal Exchange (LME) close as recent market leader copper again rallied and attacked resistance above $1,950, traders said.
Late flurries of borrowing of tight nearby spreads prompted short covering which lifted prices to unchanged levels from Thursday at $1,958, against a low of $1,919.
But despite another LME stocks fall of 8,000 tonnes benchmark three months delivery copper failed to make any significant upside inroads.
"Overall the market continues to range trade roughly between $1,900 and $2,000...its been hit by profit-taking on any upside probes," one LME floor trader commented.
Copper's near-term direction now hinges on LME warehouse stocks which currently stand at six-year lows of 123,700 tonnes.
Another fall in zinc stocks aided an earlier rally to 5-1/2 month highs of $1,075. The move was also bolstered by recent investment fund buying and uptrending charts.
Final three months business was near to this level at $1,073.50 versus $1,066.
Traders said zinc has the potential to climb further towards $1,100, although any weakening in copper prices could dent upside sentiment.
Nickel retreated after earlier relinquishing the $7,300 level under trade selling. A 90-tonne stock increase also helped to knock upside sentiment.
Physical traders said supplies of Russian nickel and stainless steel scrap are still plentiful in Western Europe.
Aluminium slipped back after a hefty 10,250-tonne stock increase. Traders said a challenge of $1,400 is seen near-term after prices lost upside momentum around $1,450.
Lead was quiet throughout and was last at $751, a loss of $1, while tin settled at $5,975, versus $5,985.
Alloy was quoted at $1,270/75, down from $1,290.

COMEX December gold ended up 10 cents at $379.20 an ounce, after trading in a $379.50-377.80 range and December silver closed down 1.0 cent at $4.798. In London gold threatened to topple to fresh lows for the year on Friday after a week of pummelling from all quarters, dealers said. Bullion fixed at $377.20 an ounce, off $2.30 from the previous fixing on Thursday afternoon and down more than $5.00 since the start of the week.
"The market looks weak and vulnerable. Everyone is having a go," a dealer said. A spate of selling last week had been linked to gold producers, a European central bank and investment funds.
